query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Microalloying equal‐atomic NbMoTaW with a controlled addition of approximately 5–10 at% Ti will enhance room‐temperature ductility by modifying the dislocation core structure and increasing grain boundary cohesion, while preserving the single‐phase BCC structure, high‐temperature (1600 °C) strength, and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal‐atomic NbMoTaW single‐phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical performance at 1600 °C and predicted irradiation resistance but very poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.intervention: Introduce a microalloying addition of 5–10 atomic percent Ti into the NbMoTaW alloy.
generation.conditions: Testing at room temperature (for ductility assessment), at 1600 °C (for high-temperature mechanical performance), and under representative irradiation conditions (to evaluate radiation damage resistance), while ensuring the alloy remains a single-phase BCC.
generation.structural_mediator: The addition of Ti is expected to remain in solid solution within the BCC matrix, altering dislocation core energies and enhancing grain boundary cohesion without triggering secondary phase formation.
generation.mechanism: Ti, a known ductilizing element with HCP-forming tendencies, is proposed to reduce the dislocation core energy and promote the activation of more favorable slip systems at room temperature. This change should increase plasticity while not interfering with the mechanisms that afford high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated NbMoTaW, the Ti-modified alloy will display significantly improved room-temperature ductility (greater plastic strain) while maintaining comparable yield strength at 1600 °C and similar irradiation resistance due to the preserved single-phase BCC structure.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only within a narrow composition window (approximately 5–10 at% Ti). Exceeding this addition may promote secondary phase formation or alter the high-temperature/irradiation performance. The hypothesis applies only if the single-phase BCC microstructure is retained.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in ductility and potential long-term stability under irradiation remain uncertain until experimental validation. Additionally, the microstructural interactions of Ti in the NbMoTaW matrix may vary based on processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: one set of equal-atomic NbMoTaW (baseline) and a second set with 5–10 at% Ti added. Process both while ensuring a single-phase BCC structure. Subject the samples to standardized mechanical tests at room temperature (e.g., tensile tests) and at 1600 °C as well as controlled irradiation experiments simulating expected service conditions.
measurements: High-temperature (1600 °C) mechanical properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength)
Microstructural characterization (XRD, TEM) to verify single-phase BCC retention and absence of secondary phases
Irradiation damage metrics (defect density, hardness changes post-irradiation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-added alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility relative to the NbMoTaW baseline, or if it exhibits a deterioration in high-temperature strength or irradiation resistance (or develops undesirable secondary phases), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure. These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C,. Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm3) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added. This resulted in RHEAs with lower densities and high-temperature strengths better than the properties of Ni-based superalloys and Fe-based steels. One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years []. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co []. First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [,]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 []. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [] and yield strength σ0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa []. decision.trend: Earlier studies on refractory high‐entropy alloys first tackled the room‐temperature brittleness by altering the microstructure via processing routes – for example, fabricating nanostructured thin films and designing an inverted two‐phase (BCC+B2) microstructure – to achieve improved ductility. More recently, researchers have linked intrinsic ductility to the atomic-scale effects of specific elemental additions: experiments and modeling (as in PMC10894205) have shown that incorporating a small fraction of elements that tend to form HCP structures can alter dislocation core properties and activate more favorable slip systems, thereby enhancing ductility. However, these approaches have not yet been applied specifically to the equal‐atomic NbMoTaW alloy, which remains a single‐phase BCC material with excellent high‐temperature strength and predicted irradiation resistance.
decision.unsolved: The unresolved challenge is to improve the room-temperature ductility of NbMoTaW without detriment to its high-temperature mechanical performance or predicted irradiation resistance, while still preserving a single-phase BCC microstructure. The question remains: Can a careful compositional tweak—without introducing secondary brittle phases—modify dislocation behavior enough to boost ductility at low temperatures?
decision.lever: Microalloying with a small percentage (e.g., 5–10 atomic %) of a ductilizing element such as Ti
decision.why: This intervention follows the trend observed in recent studies where tailored elemental additions modify dislocation core structures and promote preferred slip mechanisms that enhance room-temperature plasticity. By adding a controlled amount of Ti—a known HCP-forming element that can lower the dislocation core energy—the alloy is hypothesized to transition toward a more ductile behavior at room temperature without compromising its high-temperature strength or irradiation resistance. The low-level addition is expected to preserve the single-phase BCC structure, as supported by prior evidence on compositional tunability in refractory HEAs. An appropriate falsification experiment would be to produce NbMoTaW alloys with and without the ~5–10 at% Ti addition, then systematically compare room-temperature ductility, 1600 °C mechanical performance, and irradiation responses under controlled testing conditions.
